narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence was your plan to attend law school part-time while working. Among students who were accepted, only 7% planned to study part-time; the vast majority (93%) planned to attend full-time. This choice pushed the prediction noticeably toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 34 was the second most important factor. It sits below the average of 37.2 among accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction in the direction of passing, but not strongly enough to overcome the other influences.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.3 was the third most important feature. It is actually slightly higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it gently nudged the outcome toward passing.

In short, your part-time schedule created the largest concern for first-time bar success, outweighing the modest positive effects from your GPA and LSAT. 

To improve your chances, consider reapplying with a plan to attend full-time. Strengthening your LSAT score would also help move future predictions comfortably below the 50% threshold.
